description:
We are a creative and enthusiastic team interested in space technology, AI, web development, and Earth science. Our goal is to build an innovative and interactive project using NASA data to explore environmental changes on Earth.

We are looking for passionate teammates interested in coding, AI/ML, data analysis, web development, UI/UX design, and research. Beginners with creative ideas and a willingness to learn are also welcome.

Let's collaborate, innovate, and create something meaningful!
summary:
KEEL is a health-monitoring web app for astronauts on long-duration space missions. On a Mars-class trip, Earth can be up to 22 minutes away, so astronauts must spot changes in their own health. Radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed cabin environment cause slow changes in the immune system, bones, heart and mind that are easy to miss.

Instead of comparing crew with Earth averages, KEEL compares each astronaut with their own baseline. A heart rate of 68 bpm looks normal on a regular app, but it is a warning for an astronaut whose own normal is 46. KEEL tracks four hazard lenses, detects slow drift, explains every alert in plain language, and tells the astronaut what to do next: Watch, Act or Escalate. For serious findings it prepares a report for flight surgeons on Earth. This helps crews act early when ground support is delayed. The demo uses simulated data.
details:
What it does: KEEL monitors health indicators across four spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, closed cabin environment) and shows each astronaut how far they have drifted from their own baseline.

How it works: A drift engine calculates a personal-baseline z-score, smooths noise with an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA), and detects slow trends with CUSUM. Findings land on a triage ladder (Steady, Watch, Act, Escalate) with step-by-step on-board protocols. Every alert has a "Why am I seeing this?" panel that shows the data and the math. For serious findings, KEEL prepares a Ground Brief for flight surgeons on Earth. A built-in simulator lets users test scenarios such as a solar particle event or a CO2 leak.

Benefits and impact: Early warning of slow health decline, useful when communication with Earth is delayed by up to 22 minutes.

Tools: React, TypeScript and Vite, deployed on Vercel. The drift math is in a separate module with unit tests. Code was generated with Google Antigravity; project planning and presentation text were drafted with Claude.

Creativity: Most monitors use population-normal ranges. KEEL compares each astronaut with their own baseline and explains every alert.

Factors considered: crew privacy, color-blind-friendly status labels (color plus text), and transparency of every alert.

Limits: KEEL is a research prototype that uses simulated data. It is not a medical device, and its protocols are placeholders that would need approval by flight surgeons.
